title: Primitives, literal types, any vs unknown vs never
summary: Seven primitive types, one of them a single double-precision number type, plus literal types that turn values into types. any switches checking off, unknown forces a check, and never is the type with no values.

annotations.note: There is no int: number is Java's double / Go's float64 for everything. Integers are exact only up to Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (2^53 - 1).

The full-stack trap: Postgres bigint and Go int64 go beyond 2^53, and JSON.parse rounds to the nearest double without an error. The annotation says number and is right; the value is still wrong. Send such ids as strings.

bigint (ES2020) is arbitrary precision with its own literal suffix n. As with Go's numeric types (and unlike Java's int-to-long-to-double widening) the two never mix implicitly: tsc reports it at compile time, where plain JavaScript would throw a TypeError at run time.

A literal type is a type with one value. const keeps "GET" as its type because the binding can't change; let widens to string because it can, so a let can't be passed where only "GET" | "POST" is allowed.
The fix is an annotation with the union, not a cast: next can change, but only to a valid Method.

examples.title: string: UTF-16 code units and Turkish case mapping

annotations.note: A JS string is a sequence of UTF-16 code units, so length is not a character count and not a byte count. Go's len(s) counts UTF-8 bytes (9 here); a VARCHAR(n) in Postgres counts characters.
Unicode's default lowercase of İ (U+0130) is i followed by U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE, so the string grows by one and no longer equals "istanbul".
toLocaleLowerCase("tr") / toLocaleUpperCase("tr") apply the Turkish rules (I <-> ı, İ <-> i). Pass the locale explicitly: without an argument the result depends on the user's browser settings.
Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane (emoji, some CJK) take two code units. Spread or for...of iterates code points; slicing by index can cut one in half.

any is assignable to and from everything and allows any operation, so loose.count + 1 compiles and concatenates. Worse, any spreads: total is any too, and the missing items field is only found when the code runs.
unknown accepts every value but allows nothing until you narrow it. typeof, the null check and `"count" in v` (narrowing since TS 4.9) prove the shape step by step, then v.count is usable.
never is the empty type. A function that cannot return normally returns never, which is assignable to every type, so `return fail(...)` fits a function returning number.
An intersection of incompatible primitives reduces to never: no value is both a string and a number. The same type shows up when a switch has handled every member of a union.

use_cases: number for counts, money in minor units (kuruş) and measurements; bigint or strings for 64-bit database ids
Literal unions for closed sets of strings: HTTP methods, statuses, event names
unknown for anything from outside the program: JSON.parse, catch variables, postMessage data
never for helpers that always throw and for exhaustiveness checks
strengths: Literal types give enum-like safety to plain strings with zero runtime cost, which Java needs an enum class and Go a named type plus constants for
unknown is a safe top type: unlike Java's Object (which you downcast with a cast that may throw) you narrow with ordinary runtime checks the compiler follows
bigint and number never mix implicitly, so a precision loss can't slip in through arithmetic
weaknesses: One floating-point number type: no int, no decimal; money and 64-bit ids need care (minor units, bigint, strings)
string.length counts UTF-16 code units, which is neither Go's bytes nor the characters a user sees
any is contagious and silent, and it enters through common APIs (JSON.parse, older libraries); it takes lint rules to keep it out

pitfalls.title: Large ids through JSON.parse
pitfalls.detail: Ids above 2^53 - 1 are silently rounded. Have the server send them as strings (Go: `json:"id,string"`, SQL: id::text) and keep them as strings in TS.

pitfalls.title: toLowerCase() on Turkish text
pitfalls.detail: "ISPARTA".toLowerCase() is "isparta", and "İ".toLowerCase() has a combining dot. Use toLocaleLowerCase("tr") for Turkish user input, and plain toLowerCase() only for ASCII identifiers.

pitfalls.title: Annotating parsed JSON instead of narrowing it
pitfalls.detail: `const x: Payload = JSON.parse(s)` turns any into a promise nobody checked. Type it unknown and narrow, or validate with a schema.

pitfalls.title: Using the wrapper types
pitfalls.detail: String, Number and Boolean (capitalized) are the object wrapper types. Always write string, number, boolean.

quiz.q: `let status = "ok";` What is the type of status?
quiz.why: let can be reassigned, so the literal widens to string. const status = "ok" would have type "ok".

quiz.q: On which value can you call .toUpperCase() without any check, and have tsc accept it?
quiz.why: any disables checking (and may crash at run time); unknown requires narrowing first, for example typeof v === "string".
Outside the Turkish locale, U+0130 lowercases to i plus U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE. toLocaleLowerCase("tr") gives the single letter i.

quiz.q: A Postgres bigint id 9007199254740993 arrives as a JSON number. What does JSON.parse return?
quiz.why: JSON numbers become doubles; the nearest double to 2^53 + 1 is 2^53, and no error is raised.

further_reading.title: TypeScript Handbook: More on Functions (unknown, never)

body:
## Concept

TypeScript's primitive types are JavaScript's: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`,
`symbol`, `null` and `undefined` (always lowercase). On top of them sit **literal
types**: `"GET"`, `42` and `true` are types with exactly one value, and unions of them
(`"GET" | "POST"`) are how TypeScript models closed sets.

Three special types frame the rest of the type system:

- **`any`** opts out. Everything is assignable to it, it is assignable to everything, and
  every operation on it compiles. It is the escape hatch from untyped JavaScript.
- **`unknown`** is the safe top type. Everything is assignable to it, but you can do
  nothing with it until a runtime check narrows it.
- **`never`** is the bottom type, with no values. It is the return type of functions that
  cannot return and the type that is left after every case has been handled.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- Java/C/C++/Go: there is no `int`, `long` or `float`. `number` is a 64-bit double, and
  `bigint` is a separate arbitrary-precision type, closer to `BigInteger` than to `long`.
- Java: there are no boxed `Integer` types to think about; `String`/`Number` (capitalized)
  exist but are wrapper types you never annotate with.
- Go: a string is UTF-8 bytes there and `len` counts bytes; here a string is UTF-16
  code units, like Java's `String.length()`. Go's `strings.ToLower` ignores Turkish
  rules too (I becomes i); `strings.ToLowerSpecial(unicode.TurkishCase, s)` is its
  `toLocaleLowerCase("tr")`.
- Python: `Any` in mypy is TS's `any`; `object` is the closest thing to `unknown`;
  `NoReturn`/`Never` is `never`. `Literal["GET", "POST"]` is a literal union.
- JS: same values, same `typeof` results. TypeScript adds literal types and the three
  special types.

## Design notes

Treat `any` as a code smell to contain, not a convenience: it disables checking for
everything it touches, and it spreads through assignments and return values. At the
edges of the program (JSON, `catch`, messages from other windows) use `unknown` and
narrow once, so the types inside the program are real. Prefer literal unions to plain
`string` whenever the set of valid values is known; the next lessons show how they
replace enums. And because `number` is a double, decide deliberately how money and
database ids cross the wire: minor units as integers for money, strings for 64-bit ids.
